And when Baidu wished to bring Ghazan to his camp,
that they might eat and drink and make merry,
and rejoice in the peace that had been established between them,
Ghazan said:
"Because we have been very exhausted this night,
let us turn back a little,
and dismount and rest,
and in the morning we will gather in one place."
Now Baidu accepted this in simplicity,
and yielded to his wish.
And when he parted from Baidu and turned back,
he did not dismount from his horse,
but began travelling from the evening of that very day and the whole night,
looking behind him and marvelling at how he had been delivered from the hands of Baidu.
Now Baidu, when he returned {OCR?} to his camp,
began preparing foods and abundant gifts of every kind.
And he did not rest, nor was he quiet, nor did he sleep,
but the whole night he was in thoughts of how and in what manner he might pacify the mind of Ghazan,
and that there might be no cause of offense at all.
And as soon as the morning dawned,
he sent nobles to go and inquire after the welfare of Ghazan,
and ask him about the exhaustion and fatigue that had come upon him.
And when they went about the distance of one parasang, and two, and three, and four,
they did not find any human being at all on that road,
except perhaps exhausted horses that had been left behind,
and some of them cast down as if dead.
And thus they left off and returned,
[and] informed Baidu.
As for Baidu, he became convinced that Ghazan was offended,
and would not assent to reconciliation,
and had only turned back in order to strengthen himself,
and return again to come against Baidu.
And there came upon him great fear and no small anxiety;
and he sent word that all the nobles with their troops should gather hastily and stand against the assault of Ghazan,
when he should return to come against him.
Now Ghazan, with Nawruz the great champion, took counsel together,
and devised a plan to send and pacify the mind of Baidu,
and delay him from gathering armies and encountering Ghazan.
